title: The Sacred Heart (1673–1675)
hookLine: Margaret Mary Alacoque sees the heart of Christ burning with love

cards: A chapel in Paray-le-Monial, a small town in France. A nun of the Visitation, the order founded by Francis de Sales and Jane Frances de Chantal, kneels before the Blessed Sacrament. Her name is Margaret Mary Alacoque.

She later wrote that Jesus showed her his heart: burning with flames, ringed with thorns, a small cross rising from it. She wrote that he spoke of a heart that loved people so much and received so little love in return.
She told her superiors. They doubted her. Today, the heart she said she saw.

teach.h: A HEART ON FIRE, THORNS, A CROSS.
teach.b: First, the picture. You may have seen it on a holy card, in a kitchen, above a church door: a heart on fire, thorns around it, a cross on top, often a wound, and Jesus pointing to it with his own hand.
In the Bible the heart isn't only feelings. It's the whole inner person, where a life is decided. So for Catholics the Sacred Heart is Christ's love itself, human and divine, made visible.
Second, it's older than the chapel. Catholics root it in John's Gospel, at the cross.

teach.h: AN OPENED SIDE AT THE CROSS.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." An opened side; a heart left open.

Third, the nun who wasn't believed, until a Jesuit, Claude de la Colombière, was sent to the convent as confessor. He listened, came to trust her, and encouraged her to write down what she had received.

What she wrote asked for simple things: receiving communion on the first Friday of the month, keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and a feast day for the heart of Christ. Later, the Church made that feast its own.
In Luke's Gospel Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?"

teach.h: I AM COME TO CAST FIRE ON THE EARTH.
teach.b: The flames answer that line. Some people find the statues too sweet. Catholics who keep the devotion say it isn't sweet at all: it's a love that keeps burning when refused.

how: Catholics keep images of the Sacred Heart in homes and churches, some consecrate their families to it, parishes keep first Friday devotions, and the Church keeps the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus each year.

games.q: you're Margaret Mary. you've told your superiors what you saw in the chapel, and they doubt you. what do you do?
o: leave the convent and spread the message yourself.
stay, keep obeying, and open it to the confessor you're given.
decide you imagined it and never mention it again.
games.why: she stayed and obeyed. a Jesuit sent as confessor, Claude de la Colombière, listened, came to trust her, and encouraged her to write it down.

practice: Look at an image of the Sacred Heart, at home, at church or on your phone, and let your eyes move slowly: the flames, the thorns, the cross, the wound, the hand that points to it.
Then rest on one detail and stay there, without analyzing. If you pray, whisper his words from Luke, that it be kindled; if not, notice what that detail says to you.

wordCard.voice: Cor Iesu. Latin for heart of Jesus, the words that open most invocations in the Litany of the Sacred Heart, Christ's love pictured as a heart on fire.
